extracted.intended_audience: alert originators, EAS participants, participating CMS providers, federal/state/Tribal/territorial/local agencies, device manufacturers, utilities, emergency managers, public safety stakeholders, small businesses, and members of the public submitting comments
extracted.subtask_description: An FCC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking seeking public comment on modernizing the Emergency Alert System (EAS) and Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA), covering system objectives, who may originate alerts, transmission and resiliency requirements, message content (including multimedia and multilingual support), end-user reception, security, costs, and steps to minimize burdens on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of Alerting Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission identifies three goals: (1) alerting systems should provide authorities with the ability to rapidly notify the public of emergencies that may put the public at risk; (2) alerting systems should be capable of delivering instructions that facilitate the protection of life and property; and (3) alerting systems should provide a mechanism for government officials to provide additional authoritative communications with the public before, during, and after an emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should state whether these accurately reflect core goals and suggest additional objectives (e.g., grounding objectives in public safety outcomes such as ensuring receipt and protective action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Which Entities Should Be Authorized to Send Alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek comment on which entities (federal, state, Tribal, territorial, local) need to be able to send alerts to accomplish objectives and whether each type should be able to send alerts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how ability to send alerts at different government levels advances objectives, whether current originators undermine or support objectives, whether alerts from different sources should be reconciled to avoid duplication and alert fatigue, and proposed mechanisms for reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Alerting Capability
rubrics_metrics.description: A core purpose of EAS is enabling transmission of an emergency alert from the President or designee during a national emergency; the Commission believes that ability remains critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should address how systems should ensure Presidential capabilities are available and effective during national emergencies, including whether systems should support video messages from the President and provide estimates of incremental cost, implementation approaches, and network impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for Non-Federal Alert Originators (Local/NWS/USGS/AMBER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all day-to-day alerts are originated by non-federal agencies (e.g., NWS, USGS, state/local agencies); the Commission seeks comment on whether EAS/WEA effectively support those agencies' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address whether systems should support video messages from these agencies, identify emergencies not adequately supported, and whether incentivizing greater local use would increase life-saving alert receipt or risk alert fatigue and how to mitigate that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Governmental and Machine-to-Machine Alerting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission asks whether non-government entities (e.g., utilities) should be permitted to send safety-related alerts and whether EAS/WEA should support machine-to-machine alerting (e.g., networked sensors triggering automated protective actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should identify which non-government entities (if any) should be allowed to send alerts, in what situations, proposed levels of transparency and governmental oversight, and tradeoffs for consumer trust and resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery Reliability: Guarantee vs Best-Effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Should alerting systems be designed to guarantee delivery of each alert to intended audiences regardless of conditions, or rely on a 'best effort' approach expecting recipients may get an alert from multiple sources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify types of alerts (e.g., Presidential) that may require guaranteed delivery, and discuss implications for system design and originator confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation Requirements (Voluntary vs Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Today participation for some EAS participants and CMS providers is voluntary; the Commission seeks comment on whether voluntary participation is consistent with alerting objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss effects of voluntary participation on originator confidence, benefits and burdens of mandatory participation, and steps to balance burdens with uniformity and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resiliency and Redundancy of Transmission Pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Alerting systems should incorporate resilience to common disruptions (power outages, infrastructure damage); EAS was designed to continue operating via independently powered broadcast facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on whether EAS's original resiliency approach remains necessary, alternative communications pathways, whether EAS and WEA should each be independently resilient or provide redundancy to each other, and interoperability options to improve redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Precision and Overshoot Thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Alerting systems must be capable of delivering alerts to targeted populations without delivering to non-targeted populations; the Commission seeks comment on needed precision and what threshold of geographic overshoot would be unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess current technologies' ability to meet precision needs, potential for future improvements, how to amend rules to facilitate innovation, and whether insufficient targeting deters originator use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic/Continuous Targeting for Moving Threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Should systems be designed to support targeting alerts to a continually updated target area and people entering/leaving that area (e.g., tornadoes, wildfires)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If yes, describe technical changes required for EAS/WEA to support dynamic targeting and implications for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security, Authentication, and Public Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Alerting systems should be secure against cyberattacks that could send false alerts or block real alerts; authentication and validation measures are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss specific authentication/validation/security measures, whether visual indicators of authority would enhance trust, and tradeoffs between security, multimedia support, and delivery speed—especially during infrastructure-limited disasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory Informational Elements for WEA Alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: WEA rules require five mandatory elements in messages: the type of hazard event, the geographic area affected, a recommended protective action, the expiration time of the alert, and the identity of the sending agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission believes these elements should be supported; commenters should address whether they should be required in all alerts or whether that would be too inflexible, and suggest approaches to maximize inclusion of relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alert Message Quality, Best Practices, and Training
rubrics_metrics.description: Research shows messages that include the mandatory elements increase likelihood of protective action; many WEA messages currently lack some elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should propose resources (training, best practices) to improve message quality, uniformity, and consistency, and identify who should provide and fund such resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for Multimedia Content (Graphics/Video)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission asks whether ability to include static graphics or video would better allow alerting authorities to achieve public safety goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address technical implementation options, costs, network availability impacts, effects on device compatibility, and whether multimedia should be prioritized given tradeoffs with speed and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual Alerting Capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission seeks input on ensuring alerts effectively reach non-English-speaking populations and how multilingual capabilities should inform modernization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide proposals for integrating multilingual messaging into EAS/WEA design and discuss feasibility, priorities, and resource implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage Across Platforms and New Media
rubrics_metrics.description: Public increasingly uses platforms not equipped to interrupt content (PCs, tablets without mobile service, wearables, gaming consoles, smart speakers, streaming services, social media); the Commission asks whether existing transmission services are representative of how people consume media today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss whether EAS remains effective if limited to traditional broadcast/cable services, whether a new alerting system is needed to reach other platforms, and minimum requirements to preserve consumer trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-User Device Capability and Direct Reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Should design focus more on end-user devices' capabilities so devices can directly receive EAS messages from alerting sources regardless of user programming, enabling tailored presentation (language, font, accessibility)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on technical/procedural challenges for device manufacturers to monitor IPAWS or receive alerts directly, mitigation steps, and impacts on device costs and redesign/retooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Experience, Customization, and Tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission seeks comment on consumer frustrations with alerts, desired device features, and whether certain end-user customizations should be restricted to avoid frustrating alert originator goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address how to balance consumer choice with originator expectations, which should be prioritized in what circumstances, and how to measure tradeoffs' costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Assessment of EAS/WEA Usefulness and Need for Redesign
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission asks whether EAS and WEA are meeting needs of the public and alerting authorities, and whether aspects should be redesigned, modified, or eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify system shortcomings, elements whose costs outweigh benefits, propose eliminations or modifications, and support assertions with evidence where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future Technical Goals, Timing, and Cost Estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: What should EAS and WEA be technically capable of achieving in the next five to ten years? The Commission seeks technical steps, timelines, and cost estimates for implementation, and how to limit costs for small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative analyses, supporting data, documentation, and estimates of incremental costs (e.g., for video-rich alerts), and discuss cost-effectiveness across reform options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, Public Outreach, and Stakeholder Collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission seeks comment on how increased training for alert originators, public education, and collaboration among stakeholders can help meet alerting goals, and whether gaps exist in training or outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify gaps and who should be responsible for filling them, and whether voluntary collaboration suffices or regulatory action is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) Responses for Small Entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission prepared an IRFA and invites comments, particularly from small businesses, that are identified as responses to the IRFA and filed by NPRM deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments addressing IRFA should be separately headed. Provide estimates of economic impact, reporting/recordkeeping burdens, and proposals to minimize significant impacts on small entities (differing timetables, performance standards, exemptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Alternatives to Minimize Small Entity Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires discussion of significant alternatives such as differing compliance requirements/timetables, simplification, performance standards, or exemptions to minimize impacts on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose specific alternatives and quantify compliance cost impacts where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement to Submit Quantitative Analyses and Supporting Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters are encouraged to submit quantitative analyses, supporting data, and documentation associated with proposed modernization or redesign of EAS and WEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit cost/benefit analyses, technical documentation, and empirical evidence to support recommendations; lack of data may limit Commission's ability to evaluate proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment Filing Requirements, Methods, and Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments may be filed via the FCC's ECFS or by mail/paper filings; electronic filers should use ECFS. Comments close September 25, 2025; reply comments until October 10, 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper filers must file an original and one copy; hand-deliveries accepted 8:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m. to specified address; follow SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION for detailed instructions. People with disabilities may request reasonable accommodations via FCC504@fcc.gov or phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex Parte Rules and Filing of Presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeding is a 'permit-but-disclose' proceeding under the Commission's ex parte rules. Persons making ex parte presentations must file copies of written presentations or memoranda summarizing oral presentations within two business days (with specified content requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoranda must list attendees and summarize data/arguments; documents shown to staff count as written ex parte presentations and must be filed consistent with §1.1206(b). Where electronic filing is available, filings must be in native formats (e.g., .doc, .xml, .ppt, searchable .pdf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: This NPRM does not contain proposed information collections subject to the PRA; therefore it does not contain new or modified information collection burdens for small business concerns with fewer than 25 employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No PRA comments are solicited for new collections in this NPRM.
